title: Stiffness Measurement of Soft Silicone Substrates for Mechanobiology Studies Using a Widefield Fluorescence Microscope
protocol: Weigh out 1.75 g of the A component from the soft silicone elastomer kit.
Weigh out 1.75 g of the B component from the soft silicone elastomer kit.
Add the A component to the B component in a weighing tray.
Mix the components together for 5 min using an appropriate applicator stick.
Add the mixture to a 35 mm Petri dish.
Allow the mixture to spread evenly across the Petri dish for a couple of minutes.
Place the Petri dish with the silicone mixture, lid off, in a vacuum chamber for 15 min.
Pre-heat a hot plate to 70 °C.
Once the hot plate reaches 70 °C, place a glass slide on it.
Place the Petri dish with the silicone mixture on the glass slide.
Let the silicone cure at 70 °C for 30 min.
Place the cured soft silicone in a deep UV chamber.
Expose the soft silicone sample to deep UV light for 5 min.
Degas the deep UV chamber for at least 5 min after exposure.
Weigh out 19 mg of EDC in a microcentrifuge tube.
Add 500 μL of DI water to the EDC and dissolve by gently shaking.
Weigh out 11 mg of sulfo-NHS in a separate microcentrifuge tube.
Add 500 μL of DI water to the sulfo-NHS and dissolve by gently shaking.
Combine the EDC and sulfo-NHS solutions in a single microcentrifuge tube.
Add 30 μL of fluorescent microbeads to the EDC/sulfo-NHS solution.
Add 0.02 mg of collagen I to the EDC/sulfo-NHS/bead mixture.
Vortex the EDC/NHS/bead/collagen I mixture briefly to ensure even dispersion before coupling.
Pipette 1 mL of the EDC/NHS/bead/collagen I mixture onto a piece of parafilm placed on top of another shallow, flat lid.
Invert the Petri dish with soft silicone so that the silicone surface contacts the mixture but does not directly touch the smaller Petri dish lid below.
Raise the inverted Petri dish using one or two glass slides as spacers under either side.
Cover the sample with aluminum foil and incubate at room temperature for 30 min.
Remove the Petri dish with soft silicone and set it upright (silicone-side up).
Wash the soft silicone surface with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) by adding 2 mL of PBS (pH 7.4) to the dish.
Let the sample sit for a couple of minutes.
Aspirate off the PBS.
Wash the silicone again with 2 mL of PBS.
Place the soft silicone sample in PBS at 37 °C overnight.
Retrieve the Petri dish with soft silicone and ensure it contains at least 1 mL of PBS to have the silicone surface several mm below the liquid surface.
Using pointed tweezers, drop five 1 mm zirconium sphere indentors on the soft silicone.
Immerse the spheres into the liquid medium and drop them away from the edges of the silicone layer and at least 5 indentor diameters apart.
Place the Petri dish with soft silicone on the microscope stage for imaging through the base.
Locate and bring a sphere indentor into focus using phase imaging with a 10X objective.
Take a phase image of part or the whole of the indentor and save it.
Use a tile scan if available.
If the indentor has visible defects, discard and replace it with another indentor.
Pan to the left of the indentor’s edge so that the left edge of the frame is at least 1.5 R from the indentor center.
Ensure the center of the indentor remains visible on the right side, close to the right edge of the image frame.
Take a phase image and save it.
Switch the microscope light source to the illumination for the red fluorescent channel.
Focus down until the red fluorescent microbeads under the sphere indentor’s center just go out of focus.
Take a z-stack with an image for every z-increment of 0.5 µm.
Repeat steps with the other indentors on the sample.
Open the phase image of the indentor using ImageJ.
Click on the line tool and measure the indentor’s diameter in pixels.
Ensure that the unit of length is set to pixels by clicking Analyze | Set Scale.
Convert the indentor’s radius from pixels to μm using the CCD camera pixel size and objective magnification.
Open the red channel z-stack of microbead images in ImageJ by selecting File | Import | Image Sequence.
Select any image in the stack and click OK to open the stack.
Identify F1, the frame number where the microbeads under the indentor center are in best focus.
Identify F2, the frame number where the microbeads near the left edge of the frame at a region ~1.5 R away from the bead center are in best focus.
Calculate the indentation depth δ as the z-difference between frames F1 and F2.
Draw a line across a well-defined microbead using the line tool in ImageJ.
Click on Analyze | Plot Profile to obtain the line scan intensity profile.
Select the Live button to update the line scan intensity while choosing different frames.
Choose the frame that gives the highest value of maximum intensity as the frame in focus.
Calculate the indentation depth in μm as δ = (F2-F1) x 0.5.

Calculate the force exerted on the gel by the indenter due to its weight using the equation F = (4/3) x π x R³ x (ρindentor - ρmedium) x g, where R is the radius of the indenter, ρindentor is the density of the indenter, ρmedium is the density of the liquid medium, and g is 9.81 m/s².
Express all quantities in SI units to obtain F (in N).
Calculate Young’s modulus (E) of the silicone using a modified Hertz model equation: E = c x (3/2) x (F/(R * δ^(1.5))).
Express all quantities on the right-hand side in SI units to obtain E in Pa.
Calculate the correction factor c as follows: c = 1 - v + ((1 + v)/((9 + 7v)((1 - v)/(1 + v)) ^ (2/3))) where v is Poisson’s ratio of the silicone gel, taken as 0.5 for incompressible materials.
Calculate the height h of the soft silicone layer based on the amount of silicone added and the Petri dish diameter.
Determine the z-coordinate of the top and bottom surfaces of the silicone layer by phase imaging.
Average the Young’s modulus obtained from each indentor to obtain the mean Young’s modulus for the silicone sample.
